query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that explicitly models both high‐entropy induced lattice distortions and engineered dual‐porosity effects can more accurately identify high‐entropy alloys with very low phonon thermal conductivity (i.e., with improvements over conventional Callaway–Debye or ideal solution models) by capturing the enhanced phonon scattering from mass and strain fluctuations, which arise from severe lattice distortions intrinsic to multicomponent mixing.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloys (or ceramics) designed for thermal insulation that exhibit significant atomic size/bond strength mismatch (leading to pronounced lattice distortions) and controlled porous (dual‐porosity) microstructures.
generation.intervention: Apply the new predictive model that incorporates explicit descriptors for lattice distortions (mass and strain fluctuations) and interface scattering from dual porosity to screen candidate materials.
generation.conditions: The materials are measured under conditions where phonon conduction dominates (from room temperature to moderate-high temperatures) and where the microstructure retains the designed porosity; the model is applied to multi-element systems with a high number of principal elements and without significant secondary phase formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Severe lattice distortions from atomic size and bonding differences combined with a dual‐porosity structure that increases internal interfaces for phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced phonon scattering due to local mass and strain field fluctuations, amplified by severe lattice distortions intrinsic to multicomponent mixing and additional scattering at pore interfaces, reduces the phonon mean free path, yielding lower predicted lattice thermal conductivity than conventional models that assume ideal solution behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Materials identified by the new approach will exhibit lattice thermal conductivity values that are significantly lower (for example, >25% lower on average) than predictions made by conventional models and will more closely match experimentally measured values.
generation.baseline: Predictions from traditional models that do not fully account for disorder-induced phonon scattering (e.g., standard Callaway–Debye or ideal solution approximations).
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be accurate only for systems where the primary heat conduction is phononic and the high-entropy effects (disorder and porosity) are the dominant factors; it may not apply to alloys where additional phases, strong electronic contributions, or uncontrollable impurity phases dominate the thermal transport.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement (e.g., the exact percentage reduction in conductivity) is uncertain due to complexities in quantifying disorder and porosity effects, and experimental variations may affect direct comparisons.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high-entropy alloys (or ceramics) with designed high configurational entropy and tailored dual-porosity microstructures. Use the predictive approach to estimate their lattice thermal conductivity. Then, perform precise thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., via time-domain thermoreflectance or laser flash analysis) across a range of temperatures while characterizing lattice distortions (using XRD/HRTEM) and pore size/distribution (using SEM).
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity over the relevant temperature range
Quantitative assessment of lattice distortions and strain via diffraction/HRTEM
Pore size and porosity distribution analysis via electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivity of the tested materials deviates by more than 50% from the values predicted by the new approach, and the predictive accuracy is not demonstrably better (i.e., not showing a significant improvement over conventional models), then the hypothesis that the predictive approach accurately identifies low-phonon-thermal conductivity high-entropy materials is falsified.

Porous ceramics are often excellent materials for applications due to their low thermal conductivity [,,,]. The ultra-low thermal conductivity of porous ceramics is a primary consideration for high-temperature applications, in addition to a highly stable structure [,]. Great attention has been focused on low thermal conductivity ceramic systems, such as alumina, mullite, yttrium silicate and yttria-stabilized zirconia, which are used as insulating materials [,,,]. However, their further application at high temperatures is limited due to their lower structural stability and relatively high thermal conductivity. Hence, the development of new thermally insulating materials is necessary to cope with the high-temperature applications. Rare-earth-zirconates exhibit low thermal conductivity and good mechanical properties at room temperature, suggesting the potential of rare-earth-zirconates for applications as thermal insulation materials [,]. In recent years, due to better stability, enhanced mechanical properties and countless possibilities in composition design, high-entropy ceramics are already attracting a lot of attention [,,]. In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements.
